    Appendix

    Where to Learn More

    • ⏱️ ~2 min
    • 📚 4 sections
    • ⭐ 20 XP

    Books#

    Book Level Why read it
    The Code Book, Simon Singh Beginner A gripping history of codes and code-breaking, from Caesar to RSA
    Real-World Cryptography, David Wong Beginner → intermediate Modern protocols explained for practitioners
    Serious Cryptography (2nd edition), Jean-Philippe Aumasson Intermediate A clear, practical introduction to how modern algorithms work
    Crypto 101, Laurens Van Houtven Intermediate Free online book focused on how things break
    Bulletproof TLS and PKI, Ivan Ristić Intermediate Everything about TLS and certificates in practice
    Cryptography Engineering, Ferguson, Schneier and Kohno Intermediate How to build systems that use crypto correctly
    Security Engineering (3rd edition), Ross Anderson Intermediate Crypto inside real systems: payment cards, hardware, Kerberos and the policy fights of Chapter 20
    ✔ section read

    Courses and videos#

    • Cryptography I by Dan Boneh (Stanford, on Coursera): the classic university-level course, free to audit.
    • Introduction to Cryptography lectures by Christof Paar (free on YouTube): clear explanations with a little more math.
    • Computerphile (YouTube): short, friendly videos on many topics in this guide.
    ✔ section read

    Hands-on practice#

    • CryptoHack: a free, game-like platform for learning by breaking things.
    • Cryptopals: famous programming challenges that walk you through real attacks (ECB detection, padding oracles, and more).
    • badssl.com: test how browsers handle broken certificates.
    • The Illustrated TLS 1.3 Connection: a byte-by-byte walkthrough of a real handshake.
    • crt.sh: search Certificate Transparency logs.
    • OAuth 2.0 Playground: step through OAuth and OpenID Connect flows, including PKCE.
    • Tor Browser: see onion routing for yourself.
    • SSL Labs: grade any website's TLS setup.
    • Wireshark: watch real packets on your own network.
    ✔ section read

    Trusted references#

    • NIST Computer Security Resource Center (csrc.nist.gov): official standards (AES, SHA, ML-KEM and more).
    • OWASP Cheat Sheet Series (cheatsheetseries.owasp.org): especially "Password Storage" and "Cryptographic Storage."
    • Mozilla's Server-Side TLS guidelines and the SSL Configuration Generator.
    • Let's Encrypt documentation (letsencrypt.org/docs): how certificates and ACME work.

    Cryptography can look like magic, but it's built from a handful of simple ideas: randomness, one-way functions, shared secrets, key pairs and trust. Every padlock in your browser, every encrypted message and every app update combines the same small toolbox you've now seen from the inside.
